questions.prompt: What transaction isolation level does Postgres use by default?
choices: READ UNCOMMITTED
READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
SERIALIZABLE

query.title: Default isolation level
query.syntax:
SHOW default_transaction_isolation;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL ...;
query.explanation: Postgres defaults to READ COMMITTED, where each statement in a transaction sees a fresh snapshot taken at that statement’s start. Note Postgres has no true READ UNCOMMITTED, it is silently treated as READ COMMITTED. This differs from MySQL’s InnoDB, which defaults to REPEATABLE READ.

questions.prompt: REPEATABLE READ in Postgres can still allow certain serialization anomalies that SERIALIZABLE prevents.

query.title: REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE
query.syntax: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
query.explanation: Postgres's REPEATABLE READ gives each transaction one consistent snapshot for its whole duration, which prevents non-repeatable reads and most phantoms, but not write-skew anomalies between concurrent transactions. SERIALIZABLE adds runtime dependency tracking (SSI) to detect and abort transactions that would produce a non-serializable outcome.

questions.prompt: What mechanism lets Postgres readers avoid blocking writers (and vice versa) for the same rows?
choices: Row-level locking exclusively
MVCC (multiversion concurrency control)
Strict two-phase locking
A global read/write mutex per table

query.title: MVCC
query.syntax: -- every row carries xmin/xmax system columns
query.explanation: Rather than locking rows for reads, Postgres gives every transaction a consistent snapshot and keeps multiple versions of a row (tagged with the `xmin`/`xmax` transaction IDs that created/deleted them) around simultaneously. A reader sees the version valid for its snapshot while a writer creates a new version, so plain reads and writes rarely block each other.

questions.prompt: What does marking a CTE `WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...)` guarantee (Postgres 12+)?
choices: The CTE is computed once as its own step and not inlined/folded into the outer query
The query always runs faster
The CTE becomes a permanent table in the schema
The results are cached across separate sessions

query.title: CTE materialization fence
query.syntax: WITH name AS [MATERIALIZED | NOT MATERIALIZED] (subquery)
query.explanation: Before PG12, CTEs were always an optimization fence, computed in isolation. Since PG12 the planner may inline a CTE into the outer query like a subquery unless you force the old behavior with MATERIALIZED. This matters when a CTE with a `WHERE` filter or a volatile function needs to run exactly once rather than being pushed down.

questions.prompt: A Postgres advisory lock is tied to a specific table row and released automatically when that row is updated.

query.title: Advisory locks
query.syntax:
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(12345);
SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(12345);
query.explanation: Advisory locks are entirely application-defined: you pick an arbitrary bigint (or two ints) as the lock key, and Postgres tracks it independent of any table or row. They are commonly used to serialize application-level operations, like a single cron job across replicas, that have no natural row to lock.

questions.prompt: What does an `EXCLUDE` constraint using `gist` let you enforce that a `UNIQUE` constraint cannot?
questions.code: ALTER TABLE bookings ADD EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&);
choices: Simple column-value uniqueness
No two rows may have overlapping ranges/values for a given column, using a custom operator
Cascading foreign key deletes
Case-insensitive text uniqueness

query.title: EXCLUDE constraints
query.syntax: EXCLUDE USING gist (col1 WITH =, col2 WITH &&)
query.explanation: UNIQUE only understands equality. EXCLUDE generalizes that to any operator with a GiST or SP-GiST opclass, most commonly `&&` (overlaps) on range types, which is how you enforce "no two bookings for the same room may overlap in time" directly at the schema level instead of in application code.

questions.prompt: Which statistics does the query planner primarily use to estimate row counts for a plan?
choices: pg_stat_activity
pg_class.reltuples and the histograms/MCVs in pg_statistic
pg_locks
pg_settings

query.title: Planner statistics
query.syntax:
ANALYZE table_name;
SELECT * FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = 'table_name';
query.explanation: `ANALYZE` (run standalone or as part of autovacuum) samples the table and populates `pg_statistic` (exposed readably via the `pg_stats` view) with histograms, most-common-value lists, and null fractions per column, plus `pg_class.reltuples`/`relpages` for overall size. Stale statistics after a bulk load are a classic cause of a suddenly terrible plan.

questions.prompt: A partial index only includes rows that satisfy the `WHERE` predicate specified at index-creation time.

query.title: Partial indexes
query.syntax: CREATE INDEX idx_active ON users (id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
query.explanation: A partial index carries a `WHERE` clause baked into its definition, so rows that do not match are simply never entered into the index. This keeps the index small and fast for a common filtered access pattern (like "only active rows"), and Postgres will only use the index for queries whose `WHERE` clause the planner can prove implies the index predicate.

questions.prompt: What happens to a column value once it exceeds roughly the TOAST threshold (~2KB)?
choices: Postgres raises an error and rejects the write
It is stored out-of-line in a separate TOAST table, compressed and/or chunked
The value is silently truncated to fit
It is stored inline as base64 text

query.title: TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique)
query.syntax: SELECT pg_relation_size(reltoastrelid) FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 't';
query.explanation: Postgres pages are fixed-size (8KB by default) and a row must fit on a page, so a large value (long text, a big jsonb blob) is moved out-of-line into a hidden companion TOAST table, split into chunks, and optionally compressed first. The main table keeps only a small pointer, which is why selecting a wide column can be far slower than selecting a narrow one on the same row.

questions.prompt: What does `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` do?
choices: Waits for any locked rows, then locks and updates them
Skips over rows currently locked by another transaction instead of blocking on them
Locks every row in the table, skipping none
Disables row locking for the statement entirely

query.title: SKIP LOCKED
query.syntax: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE [SKIP LOCKED | NOWAIT]
query.explanation: Without SKIP LOCKED, a `FOR UPDATE` reader blocks until a conflicting lock is released. SKIP LOCKED instead silently excludes those rows from the result set, which is the standard building block for a job-queue pattern: several workers can each grab a different "next" row without waiting on each other.

questions.prompt: What is a HOT (heap-only tuple) update, and what must be true for Postgres to use one instead of an ordinary update?
choices: An update that skips WAL logging entirely
An update where the new row version fits on the same page and no indexed column changed, avoiding new index entries
An update performed entirely in memory without touching disk
An update that automatically triggers a VACUUM afterward

query.title: HOT updates
query.syntax: -- no special syntax; HOT is chosen automatically when eligible
query.explanation: When an UPDATE does not change any column referenced by an index and the new tuple fits in the same page (helped by fillfactor headroom), Postgres can write the new version on that page and link it from the old one via a HOT chain rather than inserting new entries into every index. That skips the index-maintenance cost of an ordinary update, and stale HOT-chain tuples get pruned opportunistically during normal page access rather than needing a full VACUUM.

questions.prompt: Transaction IDs in Postgres are a bounded 32-bit counter, so a database that never runs VACUUM can eventually wrap around and make old committed rows look like they belong to the future.

query.title: Transaction ID wraparound
query.syntax:
SELECT datfrozenxid FROM pg_database;
VACUUM (FREEZE) t;
query.explanation: Every transaction gets a 32-bit XID, and visibility is decided by comparing XIDs with wraparound arithmetic, so roughly half the ID space is treated as "in the past" at any time. Autovacuum freezes old tuples (rewriting their xmin as a special FrozenXid) so they stay visible regardless of wraparound; if autovacuum cannot keep up, Postgres starts forcing single-threaded emergency vacuums and eventually refuses new writes to protect data integrity.

questions.prompt: How does Postgres detect a deadlock between two transactions each waiting on a lock the other holds?
choices: It never detects deadlocks; both transactions hang forever
A waiter builds a wait-for graph after a timeout and cancels one transaction if a cycle is found
It relies on the operating system to detect the cycle
The client driver detects the deadlock and retries automatically

query.title: Deadlock detection
query.syntax: SET deadlock_timeout = '1s';
query.explanation: A lock waiter does not check for a deadlock immediately, it sleeps for `deadlock_timeout` first (one second by default) in case the lock simply frees up on its own. If it is still waiting after that, it builds a wait-for graph of who is blocked on whom and, if that graph contains a cycle, aborts one of the transactions in the cycle with a deadlock_detected error so the others can proceed.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `pg_advisory_lock()` and `pg_advisory_xact_lock()`?
choices: They are aliases for the same function
The session-level lock must be released explicitly (or on disconnect); the transaction-level lock releases automatically at COMMIT or ROLLBACK
pg_advisory_xact_lock only works inside stored procedures
pg_advisory_lock acquires a lock on a specific row

query.title: Advisory lock scope
query.explanation: A plain advisory lock is held by the session and stays locked across multiple transactions until you call the matching unlock function or the connection closes, which is easy to leak if a connection is pooled and reused. The transaction-scoped variant ties the lock's lifetime to the current transaction and always releases at commit or rollback, which is usually the safer default.

questions.prompt: What does Postgres streaming replication ship from primary to replica to keep it up to date?
choices: A continuous stream of WAL (write-ahead log) records
Periodic full pg_dump snapshots
SQL statements re-executed on the replica
Only the final row values via logical decoding

query.title: Streaming replication
query.syntax:
primary_conninfo = 'host=primary ...'
-- replica postgresql.conf
query.explanation: A standby connects to the primary and receives the raw WAL byte stream as it is generated, then replays those records to reproduce the exact same physical changes to its own data files. Because it replays the physical log rather than re-running statements, a physical streaming replica is byte-for-byte identical to the primary and must run the same major version.

questions.prompt: Postgres writes every data change to the write-ahead log (WAL) before applying it to the actual table/index pages on disk.

query.title: Write-ahead logging
query.syntax: SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();
query.explanation: The write-ahead-log rule is what makes crash recovery possible: a change is durably recorded in WAL (identified by a monotonically increasing log sequence number, or LSN) before the corresponding heap or index page is modified, so dirty pages can be flushed lazily because a crash before that flush can always be repaired by replaying WAL from the last checkpoint. This is the same mechanism replication reuses to stream changes to standbys.

questions.prompt: Setting `synchronous_commit = on` together with `synchronous_standby_names` changes what guarantee a COMMIT gives you compared to plain asynchronous replication?
choices: The primary waits for the named standby to acknowledge the WAL before returning success to the client
It makes replication faster by skipping WAL entirely
It guarantees the standby will never lag
It disables autovacuum on the standby

query.title: Synchronous replication
query.syntax:
synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'
synchronous_commit = on
query.explanation: With asynchronous replication a COMMIT returns as soon as the primary's local WAL write is durable, and the standby catches up whenever it can, so a primary crash can lose the last few commits. Naming a synchronous standby makes the primary block the client's COMMIT until that standby confirms it has the WAL, trading some commit latency for a guarantee that an acknowledged commit is not lost even if the primary dies immediately after.

questions.prompt: How does logical replication differ fundamentally from physical (streaming) replication?
choices: It replicates individual row changes decoded from WAL and can target specific tables, across different major versions, rather than copying identical physical bytes
It is faster because it skips WAL entirely
It requires the replica to run an older Postgres version
It can only replicate DDL, not data

query.title: Logical vs physical replication
query.syntax:
CREATE PUBLICATION pub FOR TABLE orders;
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION sub CONNECTION '...' PUBLICATION pub;
query.explanation: Physical replication ships and replays raw WAL to produce a byte-identical copy of the whole cluster. Logical replication decodes that same WAL back into a stream of row-level INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE changes (via a publication/subscription pair), so it can selectively replicate individual tables and even replicate between different major versions, at the cost of needing a primary key or replica identity to apply UPDATEs and DELETEs correctly.

questions.prompt: A single `pg_dump` run captures a consistent snapshot of the database as of one point in time, even for a database receiving concurrent writes.

query.title: pg_dump snapshot consistency
query.syntax: pg_dump -Fc mydb > mydb.dump
query.explanation: pg_dump opens one long REPEATABLE READ transaction for the whole dump, so every table it reads sees the same MVCC snapshot taken at the start, regardless of writes that commit afterward. That is why pg_dump never produces a dump with a foreign key pointing to a row that "doesn't exist yet," but it also means a dump can take a long time on a large database, holding that snapshot's resources for the duration.

questions.prompt: What is required for `pg_restore --jobs=N` to restore a database using multiple parallel workers?
choices: The dump must be in the custom (-Fc) or directory (-Fd) format, not plain SQL text
The database must already contain the schema
The dump must have been produced with --jobs as well
Nothing extra, plain SQL dumps parallelize automatically

query.title: Parallel restore
query.syntax:
pg_dump -Fd -j 4 -f dumpdir mydb
pg_restore -j 4 -d mydb dumpdir
query.explanation: Plain-text SQL dumps are just one big script executed statement by statement in order, so there is nothing to parallelize. The custom and directory archive formats store each table/index as a separate entry with dependency metadata, which lets pg_restore fan work for independent objects out across multiple worker processes and finish much faster on a multi-core machine.

questions.prompt: A 500-million-row table only gets vacuumed after roughly 100 million dead tuples accumulate, with default settings. Why?
choices: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor (default 0.2) multiplies the table's row count, so the dead-tuple threshold scales with table size, not just the fixed base threshold
Postgres caps autovacuum to once per day regardless of table size
Large tables are exempt from autovacuum
The table needs a REINDEX first

query.title: Autovacuum thresholds
query.syntax:
autovacuum_vacuum_threshold = 50
autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.2
-- trigger = threshold + scale_factor * reltuples
query.explanation: The trigger for autovacuum is threshold + scale_factor * estimated row count, so the default 0.2 scale factor means a table needs dead tuples equal to roughly a fifth of its size before autovacuum bothers, which is fine for small tables but means huge tables can accumulate a lot of bloat between vacuums. This is why large, high-churn tables commonly get a lower per-table override via ALTER TABLE ... SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01).

questions.prompt: Which built-in extension gives an accurate, direct measurement of dead-tuple bloat inside a table by physically scanning it?
choices: pg_stat_statements
pgstattuple
pg_buffercache
pg_trgm

query.title: pgstattuple for bloat
query.syntax:
CREATE EXTENSION pgstattuple;
SELECT * FROM pgstattuple('orders');
query.explanation: pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup is a statistics-collector estimate updated on each vacuum/analyze cycle, useful for a quick check but not exact. pgstattuple instead scans the actual table pages and reports precisely how many bytes are live rows, dead rows, and free space, which is the ground truth when deciding whether a table genuinely needs a VACUUM FULL or pg_repack rather than trusting a stale estimate.

questions.prompt: What does `CLUSTER orders USING orders_created_at_idx` do?
choices: Sets up multi-master clustering across servers
Physically rewrites the table so its rows are stored on disk in the order defined by that index
Creates a read replica named "orders"
Merges the table into a partition

query.title: CLUSTER
query.syntax: CLUSTER orders USING orders_created_at_idx;
query.explanation: CLUSTER rewrites the entire table in index order, which can make range scans on that index much more sequential (and cache-friendly) than the effectively-random order rows end up in after normal inserts/updates. It takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the whole rewrite, and Postgres does not maintain that physical order afterward, new rows go back to being appended wherever there is space, so the benefit erodes over time and CLUSTER has to be rerun manually.

questions.prompt: You have `WHERE city = 'Paris' AND country = 'France'`, and the planner badly overestimates how selective this is because city and country are correlated. What Postgres feature addresses this?
choices: CREATE STATISTICS with the dependencies or ndistinct kind, so ANALYZE records the actual correlation between the two columns
Adding a CHECK constraint linking the two columns
Switching the columns to a composite type
Rewriting the query as a subquery

query.title: Extended statistics
query.syntax:
CREATE STATISTICS city_country_stats (dependencies, ndistinct) ON city, country FROM locations;
ANALYZE locations;
query.explanation: By default the planner estimates multi-column selectivity by multiplying each column's independent selectivity, which badly underestimates the result size when columns are correlated (every Paris row is also a France row). CREATE STATISTICS tells ANALYZE to additionally record cross-column dependency and distinct-combination statistics, which the planner then uses instead of the naive independence assumption for that column combination.

questions.prompt: Postgres lets you define an entirely new operator symbol, like `=%`, backed by your own function, via `CREATE OPERATOR`.

query.title: Custom operators
query.syntax: CREATE OPERATOR =% (LEFTARG = text, RIGHTARG = text, FUNCTION = my_fuzzy_eq);
query.explanation: Because SQL operators in Postgres are just infix syntax bound to a function, CREATE OPERATOR lets an extension (or you) register brand-new operator symbols, or overload existing ones for new types, with commutator/negator metadata that helps the planner rewrite and optimize expressions using them. This is how extensions like PostGIS provide their own geometry operators (`&&`, `<->`, etc.) that feel native to SQL.

questions.prompt: Why does indexing a custom data type require an operator class, not just an operator?
choices: An operator class tells the index access method which operators implement comparison/ordering/overlap for that type, so it knows how to build and search the index
Operator classes are only cosmetic labels with no functional role
Every column needs its own operator class regardless of type
Operator classes replace the need for CREATE INDEX entirely

query.title: Operator classes
query.syntax: CREATE OPERATOR CLASS my_type_ops FOR TYPE my_type USING btree AS OPERATOR 1 <, OPERATOR 3 =, ...;
query.explanation: An index access method is generic, it knows how to organize a B-tree or GiST structure, but not what "less than" or "overlaps" means for an arbitrary type. An operator class is the binding that tells the access method exactly which operators and support functions to call to compare, order, or test the type, which is why every indexable type/access-method pairing (e.g. int4_ops, gist_trgm_ops) needs one, whether built in or supplied by an extension.

questions.prompt: In `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` output, what does "Buffers: shared hit=120 read=40" tell you about a plan node?
choices: 120 buffers came from the shared_buffers cache and 40 had to be read from disk (or the OS cache) for that node
120 rows were hit and 40 were missed by the WHERE clause
The query used 160MB of memory
The planner considered 160 alternative plans

query.title: EXPLAIN BUFFERS
query.syntax: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON) SELECT ...;
query.explanation: BUFFERS breaks down every page access a plan node made into hits (found already in shared_buffers, cheap) versus reads (had to be fetched, possibly hitting real disk I/O behind the OS cache). A node with a high read count relative to hit count on a repeated run is a strong signal that either the working set does not fit in shared_buffers or this data is genuinely cold, which raw timing alone would not distinguish from CPU-bound work.

questions.prompt: `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` returns the same information as text-format EXPLAIN, just serialized as a nested "Plan" object so tooling can parse it programmatically.

query.title: EXPLAIN FORMAT JSON
query.syntax: EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON) SELECT * FROM t;
query.explanation: Every plan node becomes a JSON object with keys like "Node Type", "Total Cost", and a "Plans" array of children, mirroring the indented tree text-format EXPLAIN prints, just structured instead of formatted for reading. Query-plan visualizers and automated regression tools parse this format rather than trying to regex the human-readable text output, which is unstable across versions.

questions.prompt: Why does opening a fresh Postgres connection for every web request tend to become a bottleneck as traffic grows?
choices: Postgres forks an entire OS process per connection, which is comparatively expensive to create/tear down and consumes real memory per connection regardless of activity
Postgres connections are billed per second by the server
Postgres limits every database to 10 concurrent connections
Each connection recompiles the entire query planner

query.title: Process-per-connection model
query.syntax:
-- pgbouncer.ini
pool_mode = transaction
query.explanation: Unlike a thread-per-connection design, Postgres's backend process model means each connection is a full OS process with its own memory overhead (catalog caches, local buffers) and a real fork() cost to create. That is fine at dozens of connections, but at thousands it exhausts memory and context-switching overhead, which is why a pooler like PgBouncer, that multiplexes many client connections onto a much smaller pool of real Postgres backends, is standard in production rather than connecting directly per request.

questions.prompt: Under PgBouncer's "transaction" pooling mode, what commonly breaks that works fine with a direct connection?
choices: Session-level state like prepared statements, session advisory locks, and a bare SET (without LOCAL) can leak across unrelated clients or silently vanish, since the underlying server connection is only borrowed for one transaction
Transactions can no longer be rolled back
INSERT statements stop working
The database name can no longer be specified

query.title: Pooling mode tradeoffs
query.syntax:
-- pgbouncer.ini
pool_mode = transaction   -- vs session, statement
query.explanation: In transaction mode, PgBouncer only dedicates a real server connection to a client for the duration of one transaction, then returns it to the pool for someone else, which lets a small number of backends serve far more clients. The cost is that anything tied to the session rather than the transaction, a PREPAREd statement, a session advisory lock, a bare SET without LOCAL, can end up visible to, or missing from, the next unrelated client that borrows the same underlying connection.

questions.prompt: A transaction running under SERIALIZABLE isolation fails with SQLSTATE 40001. What should the application do?
choices: Treat it as a permanent error and give up

Retry the entire transaction from the beginning; the failure means Postgres could not prove the concurrent history was equivalent to some serial order, not that anything is actually wrong with the data
Switch to READ UNCOMMITTED and retry
Manually run VACUUM before retrying

query.title: Serialization failure handling
query.syntax: -- SQLSTATE 40001: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions
query.explanation: SERIALIZABLE in Postgres uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): transactions run under normal MVCC snapshots, but a background mechanism tracks read/write dependencies between concurrent transactions and aborts one if it detects a cycle that would make the outcome non-serializable. Because the abort is about a scheduling conflict, not corrupted data, the correct and normal response is simply to retry the whole transaction, which is why every serializable-mode client library expects and implements a retry loop around 40001.

questions.prompt: What does the `pg_stat_statements` extension track?
choices: Per-normalized-query execution statistics (calls, total/mean time, rows, buffer usage) aggregated across all executions with the same query shape, literals replaced by placeholders
A live feed of currently running queries
A history of every DDL change ever made
Row-level audit logs of every UPDATE

query.title: pg_stat_statements
query.explanation: Rather than logging every individual execution, pg_stat_statements normalizes each query by replacing literal constants with parameter placeholders, buckets executions by that normalized shape, and accumulates counters like call count, total/mean/max time, and rows returned per bucket. That is what lets you ask "which query shape is costing the most total time across the whole workload" instead of drowning in per-execution log lines, at the cost of needing it preloaded at server start since it needs shared memory allocated up front.

questions.prompt: What actually happens when you run `CREATE EXTENSION hstore;`?
choices: Postgres downloads the extension source from the internet and compiles it on the fly
Postgres reads the extension's already-installed control file and SQL script and executes that script to create its objects inside the current database, tracked as one unit
It only adds a comment to the catalog with no functional change
It creates a new physical database dedicated to the extension

query.title: Extension mechanism
query.syntax:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS hstore;
\dx  -- list installed extensions
query.explanation: An extension's files (a .control file plus one or more versioned .sql scripts, and often a compiled .so for C code) must already be present in the server's share directory, typically via an OS package like postgresql-contrib, before CREATE EXTENSION can do anything. The command itself just runs the matching SQL script against the current database and registers the whole resulting set of objects as one extension, so DROP EXTENSION or ALTER EXTENSION UPDATE can manage them together instead of you tracking each object by hand.

questions.prompt: What does `postgres_fdw` let you do?
choices: Query tables on a remote Postgres server as if they were local tables, with the planner able to push some filtering/joining work to the remote side
Convert a Postgres table into a foreign key automatically
Replicate a table across data centers automatically
Encrypt foreign key columns

query.title: Foreign data wrappers
query.syntax:
CREATE SERVER remote_srv FOREIGN DATA WRAPPER postgres_fdw OPTIONS (host '...', dbname '...');
CREATE FOREIGN TABLE remote_orders (...) SERVER remote_srv;
query.explanation: The foreign data wrapper (FDW) API lets an extension present an external data source as ordinary-looking tables inside a local database. postgres_fdw is the reference implementation for talking to another Postgres server, and a reasonably smart one, it can push WHERE clauses, joins, and even some aggregates down to execute on the remote server rather than pulling every row across the network first. Other FDWs exist for CSV files, other databases, and various APIs, all through the same extensible interface.

questions.prompt: With classic (non-partitioned) table inheritance, a UNIQUE constraint on the parent table is automatically enforced across all child tables combined.

query.title: Inheritance constraint limits
query.syntax:
CREATE TABLE measurement (...);
CREATE TABLE measurement_2024 () INHERITS (measurement);
query.explanation: Classic inheritance only shares column definitions and lets queries against the parent transparently scan children too; it does not give you a cross-child UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, or foreign key, each child table's constraints (if any) are enforced independently within that one table. This is one reason declarative partitioning, which does support a unique index across the whole partitioned table when it includes the partition key, largely superseded inheritance for splitting one logical table across many physical ones.

questions.prompt: What is a key advantage declarative partitioning (`PARTITION BY RANGE/LIST/HASH`) has over old-style table inheritance for splitting a large table?
choices: The planner has first-class awareness of partitions and can prune irrelevant ones automatically, and routing an INSERT to the correct partition is automatic instead of needing trigger-based routing
Partitioned tables have no row limit while inherited tables do
Partitioning removes the need for indexes on child tables
Partitioning replicates data automatically across partitions

query.title: Partitioning vs inheritance
query.syntax:
CREATE TABLE measurement (...) PARTITION BY RANGE (logdate);
CREATE TABLE measurement_y2024 PARTITION OF measurement FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2025-01-01');
query.explanation: Old-style inheritance needed a hand-written trigger or rule to route an INSERT to the right child table and gave the planner no special knowledge of the split. Declarative partitioning builds routing and pruning into the core engine: an INSERT is automatically sent to the matching partition, and the planner can eliminate whole partitions from a query plan at planning (or even execution) time when the WHERE clause is incompatible with a partition's bounds.

questions.prompt: Why can partition pruning sometimes only happen at execution time rather than planning time?
choices: When the partition key is compared against a bind parameter or a subquery result rather than a literal constant, the planner cannot know which partitions qualify until the value is actually known, so pruning is deferred to execution
Execution-time pruning is always disabled by default
Partition pruning only ever happens at planning time
Partition pruning requires manually calling a pruning function

query.title: Partition pruning timing
query.syntax: PREPARE q(date) AS SELECT * FROM measurement WHERE logdate = $1;
query.explanation: If a query filters the partition key against a literal constant, the planner can figure out at plan time which partitions could possibly match and skip generating scan nodes for the rest. If the comparison value is a bind parameter, a volatile function, or a subquery result, that value is not known until the query actually runs, so Postgres instead defers pruning to execution time, still skipping the irrelevant partitions' actual scans, just one step later than the ideal case.

questions.prompt: What is a hard limit on `NOTIFY channel, payload` that makes it unsuitable as a general message queue?
choices: The payload is capped at 8000 bytes, and notifications are only visible to listeners that were connected at commit time, with no persistence or delivery guarantee otherwise
NOTIFY can only be called from a superuser session
Only one LISTEN per database is allowed at a time
NOTIFY blocks until every listener acknowledges receipt

query.title: LISTEN/NOTIFY limits
query.syntax:
LISTEN orders_channel;
NOTIFY orders_channel, 'order:123';
query.explanation: NOTIFY is a lightweight, fire-and-forget pub/sub mechanism scoped to one database: the payload is limited to 8000 bytes, delivery only happens to sessions that were actively listening when the notifying transaction commits (nothing is queued for a client that connects afterward), and there is no acknowledgment or retry. It is great for cheaply waking up a worker ("something changed, go check the table") but the actual durable state has to live in a real table, not in the notification payload.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a checkpoint, and what do `max_wal_size` and `checkpoint_timeout` control about it?
choices: A checkpoint flushes all dirty pages to disk and marks a point WAL replay can start from after a crash; max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout bound how much WAL (or how much time) can accumulate before the next checkpoint is forced
A checkpoint deletes old rows to save space
A checkpoint rebuilds every index in the database
A checkpoint disconnects idle client connections

query.title: Checkpoints
query.syntax:
checkpoint_timeout = 5min
max_wal_size = 1GB
query.explanation: Crash recovery replays WAL starting from the most recent checkpoint, so the more WAL has accumulated since then, the longer recovery takes. A checkpoint writes all currently-dirty shared buffer pages out to the actual data files so WAL before that point is no longer needed for recovery; checkpoint_timeout triggers one on a time basis and max_wal_size triggers one once that much WAL has been generated, whichever comes first, trading write I/O spikes during checkpoints against recovery time and WAL disk usage.

questions.prompt: `full_page_writes = on` exists to protect against a "torn page," where an OS/storage crash writes only part of an 8KB page before power loss.

query.title: Full page writes
query.syntax: full_page_writes = on   -- default
query.explanation: Disk writes are not guaranteed atomic at the 8KB page granularity Postgres uses, a crash mid-write can leave a page half-old, half-new. With full_page_writes on, the first change to a page after each checkpoint logs the entire page image to WAL, not just the diff, so recovery can restore that page to a known-good state before replaying subsequent record-level changes on top. Turning it off is only safe on storage that itself guarantees atomic page writes, which is rare enough that it stays on by default.

questions.prompt: A query has been running for a while and `pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type` shows "Lock" with `wait_event` "relation". What is that query doing?
choices: Actively using CPU to scan the relation
Blocked, waiting to acquire a lock on a relation held by another session
Waiting for a client-side network read
Running a background vacuum

query.title: pg_stat_activity wait events
query.syntax: SELECT pid, wait_event_type, wait_event, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';
query.explanation: wait_event_type categorizes what a backend is currently blocked on (Lock, LWLock, IO, Client, etc.), and wait_event gives the specific name within that category. "Lock"/"relation" means the backend is parked waiting for a heavyweight table-level lock that some other session currently holds, which is the first place to look, via pg_locks joined back to pg_stat_activity, to find the blocking session rather than assuming the query itself is just slow.

questions.prompt: Why does `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` avoid blocking regular reads and writes on the table, unlike a plain `CREATE INDEX`?
choices: It takes a weaker lock (SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE) that does not conflict with ordinary SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, by building the index in multiple passes instead of one exclusive scan
It builds the index entirely in memory with no disk writes
It skips validating existing rows
It only works on empty tables

query.title: CONCURRENTLY and lock strength
query.syntax: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx ON t (col);
query.explanation: A plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock that blocks writers for the whole build. CONCURRENTLY instead takes the much weaker SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock and does the work in several separate transactions/passes, so it does not exclude concurrent writes, at the cost of a longer overall build time and the possibility of being left in an unusable "invalid" state if it is interrupted, which then requires dropping and retrying it.

questions.prompt: What is `PREPARE TRANSACTION` used for?
choices: Precompiling a query plan for reuse

The first phase of a two-phase commit: it durably records a transaction as ready to commit without actually committing it, so an external coordinator can commit or roll it back later, even across a server restart
Preparing a parameterized statement for a prepared statement
Scheduling a transaction to run at a future time

query.title: Two-phase commit
query.explanation: Two-phase commit exists for distributed transactions spanning multiple databases: each participant PREPAREs (durably persists all its work as pending, disconnecting the transaction from the session that started it), and only once every participant has successfully prepared does the coordinator tell each one to COMMIT PREPARED. This is what lets a coordinator recover and finish correctly even if it crashes between preparing and committing, at the operational cost that a prepared transaction left dangling holds locks and blocks vacuum until resolved.

questions.prompt: A long-running query can fail with a "snapshot too old" error if `old_snapshot_threshold` is configured and enough time has passed for older row versions it still needs to have been vacuumed away.

query.title: Snapshot too old
query.syntax: old_snapshot_threshold = 60   -- minutes
query.explanation: Normally Postgres keeps dead-but-still-visible-to-someone row versions around until nothing needs them, which can bloat a table if one connection holds a snapshot open for a long time. old_snapshot_threshold trades that safety for space: it tells vacuum it is allowed to remove tuples older than the configured age even if a snapshot might still need them, and a query that then tries to use such an old snapshot gets an explicit "snapshot too old" error instead of silently wrong results.

questions.prompt: What must be true for Postgres to satisfy a query with an index-only scan, never touching the underlying heap page at all?
choices: Every column the query needs is present in the index, and the visibility map shows the relevant heap pages are "all visible" so per-tuple visibility does not need to be rechecked against the heap
The table must have no indexes other than the one used
The query must use SELECT *
Index-only scans never need the visibility map

query.title: Index-only scans
query.syntax:
CREATE INDEX ON t (a, b);
EXPLAIN SELECT a, b FROM t WHERE a = 1;  -- look for "Index Only Scan"
query.explanation: An index normally only proves a row exists at some heap location, Postgres still visits the heap to confirm the row is actually visible to the current transaction's snapshot. The visibility map tracks, per heap page, whether every tuple on it is known-visible to everyone (set by VACUUM), and when that bit is set and the index already contains every column the query needs, the heap fetch can be skipped entirely, which is why a table that never gets vacuumed loses this optimization even with a perfectly matching index.

questions.prompt: When is a BRIN (Block Range INdex) a better fit than a B-tree?
choices: On a very large table where the indexed column is naturally correlated with physical row order (like an ever-increasing timestamp), trading precision for a tiny index that only stores min/max summaries per block range
When you need exact equality lookups on a low-cardinality column
When the table is small and fits entirely in memory
When you need the index to enforce uniqueness

query.title: BRIN indexes
query.syntax: CREATE INDEX ON events USING brin (created_at);
query.explanation: A BRIN index does not store an entry per row, it stores one small summary (like a min/max range) per physical block range, making it orders of magnitude smaller than a B-tree on a huge table. That only works well when the column’s values correlate with physical storage order, so a range scan can use the summaries to skip whole block ranges that cannot contain a match; on an uncorrelated column it degrades to scanning nearly everything anyway.

questions.prompt: Structurally, what does a GIN index store that lets it efficiently answer "does this array/jsonb/tsvector contain value X"?
choices: A single sorted list of whole row values, like a B-tree
An inverted index: one entry per distinct component value, each pointing to a posting list of every row containing it
A hash of the entire column value
A compressed copy of the full column

query.title: GIN internals
query.syntax:
CREATE INDEX ON docs USING gin (body_tsv);
CREATE INDEX ON t USING gin (tags);
query.explanation: GIN decomposes a composite value, the words in a tsvector, the elements of an array, the keys/values of a jsonb document, into its individual components and builds one inverted-index entry per distinct component, each entry listing every row that contains it. That is the same structure a search engine uses, and it is exactly why GIN excels at "contains" queries (`@>`, `?`, full-text `@@`) but is comparatively slow to update, since a single row change can touch many posting lists.

questions.prompt: What does adding `INCLUDE (total)` to `CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total)` accomplish that a plain index on `customer_id` alone would not?
choices: total is stored in the index leaf pages (not part of the sort key) so a query selecting customer_id and total can be answered as an index-only scan without adding total to the key
It sorts the index by total as a secondary key
It makes the index enforce uniqueness on total
It compresses the total column

query.title: Covering indexes (INCLUDE)
query.syntax:
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (total);
SELECT customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1;
query.explanation: INCLUDE columns ride along in the index’s leaf pages as extra payload without being part of the B-tree’s sort/search key, so they neither help nor hurt the lookup itself but do let more queries qualify for an index-only scan by having every needed column available right there. This is useful when you would otherwise be tempted to add a column to the key purely to widen index-only-scan coverage, which would also bloat the internal tree nodes that only need the actual search key.

questions.prompt: A table shows a high `n_dead_tup` relative to `n_live_tup` in `pg_stat_user_tables` right before autovacuum is due to run. What does that indicate?
choices: A large fraction of the table’s rows are stale versions from UPDATE/DELETE waiting to be reclaimed, meaning queries are scanning more physical rows than the "logical" row count suggests
The table has too many indexes
The table's data is corrupted
Replication has fallen behind

query.title: n_dead_tup
query.syntax: SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables;
query.explanation: Every UPDATE creates a new row version and leaves the old one as a dead tuple until vacuumed; every DELETE leaves a dead tuple outright. n_dead_tup is the statistics collector’s running estimate of how many such dead versions currently sit in the table, and a high ratio relative to live rows means sequential scans (and even index scans that still visit the heap) are wasting work skipping over them, which is the practical symptom of the "bloat" autovacuum exists to control.

questions.prompt: Why can one client that opens a transaction, runs one query, and then sits idle for hours (without committing) cause vacuum on unrelated, busy tables to stop reclaiming space?
choices: That transaction still holds an old snapshot, which pins the oldest XID Postgres must still treat as "possibly visible to someone," so vacuum anywhere in the database cannot remove any tuple newer than that XID until the transaction ends
It locks every table in the database explicitly
It only affects the specific table it queried
Idle transactions have no effect on vacuum

query.title: idle in transaction and vacuum
query.syntax: SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min';
query.explanation: Vacuum can only remove a dead tuple once it is certain no live snapshot could still need to see it, and the oldest still-open snapshot in the whole database sets that boundary regardless of which table it queried or is even touching right now. A forgotten "idle in transaction" session therefore holds back that boundary globally, which is why it is a classic cause of sudden, database-wide bloat and why idle_in_transaction_session_timeout is a common production safeguard.

questions.prompt: If a replica using a physical replication slot disconnects and never reconnects, the primary will keep accumulating WAL on disk indefinitely to satisfy that slot, potentially filling the disk.

query.title: Replication slots and WAL retention
query.syntax: SELECT slot_name, active, pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn) FROM pg_replication_slots;
query.explanation: A replication slot exists precisely to guarantee the primary retains WAL back to whatever point that consumer still needs, even across a disconnect, so the consumer can always resume without gaps. That guarantee has no automatic time or size limit by default: a slot for a replica that never comes back keeps pinning WAL forever, which is why monitoring restart_lsn lag (or using PG13+'s max_slot_wal_keep_size) matters, an abandoned slot is a very common cause of a primary's disk unexpectedly filling up.

questions.prompt: By default, does a Row Level Security policy on a table apply to the table's owner?
choices: No, table owners bypass RLS by default unless the table has FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY set
Yes, RLS always applies to every role including the owner with no way to change that
RLS only ever applies to superusers
RLS policies apply only to SELECT, never to owners running UPDATE

query.title: Row level security and ownership
query.explanation: RLS is meant to restrict application-level roles, so by default the table owner (and superusers) can see everything regardless of policies, on the assumption the owner already has full DDL control over the table anyway. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY closes that exception and makes policies apply even to the owner's own queries, which matters if the same role that owns the table also runs application queries against it.

questions.prompt: Rolling back a transaction that called `nextval()` on a sequence puts the consumed value back so the next call reuses it.

query.title: Sequences are non-transactional
query.explanation: Sequences are deliberately excluded from transactional rollback so that two concurrent transactions can call nextval() without blocking each other waiting to see whether the other commits; if sequence advances were transactional, every insert into a SERIAL column would serialize on the sequence. The tradeoff is that any rolled-back transaction, or a server crash after a few values were cached, leaves permanent gaps in the sequence, which is normal and expected, not a sign something is broken.

questions.prompt: What is one practical advantage of `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` over `SERIAL` for a primary key column?
choices: It is SQL-standard syntax, and with GENERATED ALWAYS it rejects a plain manual INSERT into that column unless the caller explicitly opts in with OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE, preventing accidental collisions with the sequence
Identity columns can be updated directly without any restriction, unlike SERIAL
Identity columns do not use a backing sequence at all
Identity columns are always faster to insert into

query.title: Identity columns
query.explanation: SERIAL is just a default expression calling nextval(), so nothing stops a plain INSERT INTO t (id) VALUES (5) from writing a value that later collides with the sequence’s own next value. GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY actively rejects a bare manual value in that column, requiring the explicit OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE clause to do so on purpose, which closes a whole class of "someone hardcoded an id and now the sequence is out of sync" bugs, on top of being the syntax the SQL standard defines rather than a Postgres-only convention.

questions.prompt: In a window function, what is the practical difference between a `ROWS BETWEEN` frame and a `RANGE BETWEEN` frame?
choices: ROWS counts a fixed number of physical rows before/after the current row; RANGE instead measures by the value of the ORDER BY expression, grouping "peer" rows with equal ordering values into the same frame boundary
They are exact synonyms with no behavioral difference
RANGE only works with integer columns
ROWS ignores the ORDER BY clause entirely

query.title: Window frame modes
query.syntax:
SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1 day' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
query.explanation: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW always spans exactly three physical rows. RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1 day' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW instead defines the frame by value distance along the ORDER BY key, so rows with the same ordering value are always frame-peers together, and a numeric or interval offset lets you express "the last 24 hours of rows" directly rather than an arbitrary row count that may not correspond to any fixed time span.

questions.prompt: What happens if you write a `WITH RECURSIVE` query over a graph with a cycle and forget a termination/visited-check condition?
choices: Postgres automatically detects the cycle and stops after one pass
The recursive query loops until resources run out, since Postgres does not detect cycles on its own, unlike SQL's optional CYCLE clause (PG14+) which must be explicitly requested
It raises a compile-time error before running
It silently returns zero rows

query.title: WITH RECURSIVE cycles
query.syntax:
WITH RECURSIVE search_graph(id, path, is_cycle) AS (
  SELECT id, ARRAY[id], false FROM nodes WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n.id, path || n.id, n.id = ANY(path)
  FROM nodes n JOIN search_graph g ON n.parent = g.id
  WHERE NOT is_cycle
)
SELECT * FROM search_graph;
query.explanation: A recursive CTE just keeps re-executing its recursive term against the previous iteration's output until that output is empty; nothing inherently stops it from revisiting the same node forever if the underlying data has a cycle. You have to track visited nodes yourself (commonly with an accumulating array and a WHERE NOT already_visited check) or, from PG14 on, use the standard SEARCH ... CYCLE clause, which does this bookkeeping for you.

questions.prompt: What does the `LATERAL` keyword let a subquery in the FROM clause do that a plain subquery cannot?
choices: Reference columns from FROM items that appear earlier in the same FROM clause, effectively running once per row of the preceding item
Run before the rest of the query starts, at parse time
Replace the need for a JOIN entirely
Automatically parallelize the subquery

query.title: LATERAL joins
query.explanation: An ordinary subquery in FROM is evaluated once, independently of anything else in the query, so it cannot reference `c.id` from another table in the same FROM list. Marking it LATERAL allows exactly that: the subquery is conceptually re-evaluated for each row from the preceding FROM item, which is the standard way to express "top N per group" without a window function, or to call a set-returning function with arguments taken from an earlier table.

questions.prompt: `CREATE AGGREGATE` lets you define an entirely new aggregate function by supplying a state-transition function and a final function, without writing any C code.

query.title: Custom aggregates
query.explanation: An aggregate in Postgres is defined declaratively as a state type plus a transition function (called once per input row to fold it into the running state) and, optionally, a final function to transform the accumulated state into the result. All three pieces can be ordinary SQL or PL/pgSQL functions, which is how you get a fully custom GROUP BY-compatible aggregate, such as concatenating arrays across rows, without touching Postgres’s internals or writing an extension in C.

questions.prompt: Why is wrapping a PL/pgSQL statement in `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN ... END` inside a loop that runs millions of times a common performance mistake?
choices: Each EXCEPTION block establishes a subtransaction, which has real overhead to set up and tear down even when no exception is raised
EXCEPTION blocks are purely cosmetic and have zero runtime cost
PL/pgSQL forbids EXCEPTION blocks inside loops
It disables all indexes for the duration of the loop

query.title: PL/pgSQL exception handling cost
query.explanation: Any block with an EXCEPTION clause implicitly opens a subtransaction so a failure inside it can be rolled back to a savepoint without aborting the whole outer transaction. That subtransaction machinery has a real, measurable cost, and paying it a million times in a tight loop, most of which never actually raise, is why bulk operations are usually restructured to catch the exceptional case in bulk (e.g. ON CONFLICT) rather than wrapping every single iteration defensively.

questions.prompt: What is an event trigger, as distinct from a regular (DML) trigger?
choices: A trigger that fires on DDL events (like CREATE TABLE or DROP) or other database-wide events, rather than on row/statement-level INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE against one table
A trigger that fires on a schedule, like a cron job
A synonym for a per-row AFTER trigger
A trigger that only fires on client connect/disconnect

query.title: Event triggers
query.syntax: CREATE EVENT TRIGGER audit_ddl ON ddl_command_end EXECUTE FUNCTION log_ddl();
query.explanation: Regular triggers are attached to one table and fire on data changes to that table. Event triggers are database-wide and fire on schema-level events like ddl_command_start/ddl_command_end or sql_drop, which is how you can, for example, log every DDL statement executed anywhere in the database, or block certain DDL patterns outright, something a per-table DML trigger has no way to observe.

questions.prompt: Why does inserting a row with a foreign key reference take a lock on the referenced parent row, and specifically why is it `FOR KEY SHARE` rather than a full row lock?
choices: The insert needs to ensure the parent row is not deleted or have its key changed before commit, but FOR KEY SHARE is deliberately the weakest lock that still allows concurrent non-key updates to the parent row
Foreign keys never lock the parent row at all
It takes the strongest lock, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, on the parent row
The lock is only taken at COMMIT time, not on INSERT

query.title: Foreign key locking
query.syntax:
-- implicit when inserting a row that references parent.id
SELECT 1 FROM parent WHERE id = $1 FOR KEY SHARE;
query.explanation: To guarantee referential integrity, an insert (or update) that creates a foreign key reference must be sure the referenced row still exists and keeps the same key value until commit, which requires locking it in some form. FOR KEY SHARE is designed to be the least restrictive lock that still protects the key columns: it conflicts with someone deleting or changing the key of that row, but not with an ordinary UPDATE that only touches unrelated columns, so foreign keys do not needlessly serialize unrelated writes to the parent.

questions.prompt: What does declaring a constraint `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` change compared to the default (immediate) checking?
choices: The constraint is checked at COMMIT time instead of after each individual statement, which allows temporarily-violating intermediate states within one transaction
The constraint is never actually enforced
It makes the constraint apply only to future rows
It converts a CHECK constraint into a trigger automatically

query.title: Deferrable constraints
query.explanation: By default a UNIQUE or foreign key constraint is checked immediately after the statement that could violate it, which makes some perfectly-fine-by-commit-time operations, like swapping two rows’ unique values in two statements, fail partway through. Marking the constraint DEFERRABLE (and INITIALLY DEFERRED, or calling SET CONSTRAINTS ... DEFERRED within the transaction) postpones the check to COMMIT, so only the final state has to satisfy the constraint, not every intermediate statement.

questions.prompt: Why is `pg_upgrade --link` (link mode) dramatically faster than the default copy mode for a large database?
choices: It uses hard links to the old cluster's data files instead of physically copying them, so the upgrade's time is roughly independent of database size, at the cost of making the old cluster unusable once you start the new one
It skips upgrading indexes entirely
It runs entirely on the standby without touching the primary
It only works for databases under 1GB

query.title: pg_upgrade link mode
query.syntax: pg_upgrade --link -b oldbindir -B newbindir -d olddatadir -D newdatadir
query.explanation: Copy mode duplicates every table and index file byte-for-byte into the new cluster's data directory, which for a large database means an upgrade that takes as long as copying the whole dataset. Link mode instead creates hard links, additional directory entries pointing at the exact same files on disk, so no data is physically copied and the upgrade finishes in roughly constant time regardless of database size; the tradeoff is that the old and new clusters now share the underlying files, so starting the old cluster again after using the new one can corrupt both.

questions.prompt: What role does an output plugin (like `pgoutput` or `wal2json`) play in logical replication?
choices: It decodes the raw, binary WAL record stream into a structured, plugin-defined representation of the logical row changes, which is what a subscriber or external consumer actually reads
It compresses WAL files for storage
It replaces the need for a replication slot
It only works for DDL changes, not DML

query.title: Logical decoding output plugins
query.syntax: SELECT * FROM pg_logical_slot_get_changes('my_slot', NULL, NULL);
query.explanation: Physical WAL records are low-level and version/build-specific, not something an external consumer should parse directly. Logical decoding runs WAL through an output plugin that reconstructs the logical INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations those bytes represent and emits them in whatever format that plugin defines, pgoutput (used internally by native logical replication) emits a compact binary protocol, while wal2json emits human-readable JSON for external tools like Debezium to consume.

questions.prompt: A table has no primary key and no unique index. What happens when you try to UPDATE or DELETE a row on it through logical replication?
choices: It fails (or is disallowed) because logical replication needs a REPLICA IDENTITY to identify which row on the subscriber to apply the change to, and the default replica identity is the primary key
It works exactly the same as with a primary key
It silently updates a random row
It automatically falls back to physical replication for that table

query.title: Replica identity
query.syntax: ALTER TABLE t REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;   -- or USING INDEX some_unique_idx
query.explanation: A physical replica just replays byte-identical page changes and never needs to "identify a row", but logical replication ships row-level changes that must be matched against the corresponding row on a possibly-different physical layout on the subscriber. That match needs a way to uniquely identify the old row, which defaults to the primary key; without one (and without an explicit REPLICA IDENTITY FULL or a designated unique index) UPDATE/DELETE changes on that table cannot be replicated correctly.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between `CREATE PUBLICATION` and `CREATE SUBSCRIPTION`?
choices: A publication (defined on the sender) names which tables/changes to expose; a subscription (defined on the receiver) connects to a publication and applies the changes it streams
They are two names for the same object created on the same server
A publication is required only for DDL replication
A subscription must be created before its publication exists

query.title: Publication and subscription
query.explanation: The publisher-side CREATE PUBLICATION is metadata declaring which tables (and which operation types) are exposed for logical replication, it does no networking on its own. CREATE SUBSCRIPTION on the receiving side actually establishes a replication connection to the publisher, requests an initial data sync, and then continuously applies the streamed changes, so the two statements run on different servers and play complementary roles.

questions.prompt: How does `pg_repack` shrink a bloated table without the long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that VACUUM FULL or CLUSTER require?
choices: It builds a new, compact copy of the table alongside the old one while capturing concurrent changes via a log table, then swaps the two with only a brief exclusive lock at the very end
It rewrites the table in place one page at a time with no locking at all
It only defragments indexes, never touches heap pages
It requires taking the whole database offline

query.title: pg_repack
query.syntax: pg_repack -d mydb -t orders
query.explanation: VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER both rewrite a table by locking it exclusively for the entire operation. pg_repack instead creates a new table, copies the existing rows into it, and uses a trigger to capture any concurrent writes that happen during that copy into a log table which it then replays, so almost all of the work happens with the original table still fully readable and writable; only the final atomic swap of the old and new table needs a brief exclusive lock.

questions.prompt: What does `max_parallel_workers_per_gather` control, and why might a query you expect to be parallelized still run with a single worker?
choices: It caps how many parallel worker processes one Gather node can request; the planner can still choose fewer if the estimated cost does not clear the parallel setup/tuple cost, or if the query is unsafe to parallelize
It sets the maximum number of concurrent client connections allowed
It has no effect on planning, only execution
It guarantees every query will use exactly that many workers

query.title: Parallel query workers
query.syntax:
SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 4;
EXPLAIN SELECT count(*) FROM huge_table;
query.explanation: Parallel workers are not free, spawning them has real setup cost the planner weighs via parallel_setup_cost and parallel_tuple_cost against the estimated benefit, so a query over a small (or misestimated-as-small) table can legitimately be planned to run serially even with a high worker limit configured. Parallelism is also only available for plan shapes the executor supports splitting, so a query built around something inherently sequential, like a correlated subquery calling a non-parallel-safe function, will not parallelize regardless of the setting.

questions.prompt: What triggers Postgres to JIT-compile expressions in a query plan rather than interpreting them?
choices: The planner's estimated total query cost exceeding jit_above_cost, so JIT is skipped for cheap queries where compilation overhead would outweigh any speedup
JIT compilation happens for every query unconditionally once the jit extension is installed
JIT only applies to DDL statements
JIT is triggered by the number of rows actually returned, discovered after execution finishes

query.title: JIT compilation
query.syntax:
SET jit_above_cost = 100000;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT ...;  -- look for "JIT:" section
query.explanation: JIT-compiling a query’s expressions and tuple-deforming logic into native machine code takes real time up front, which only pays off if the query then does enough work to amortize it. Postgres gates JIT behind estimated cost thresholds (jit_above_cost to JIT at all, higher thresholds to additionally inline called functions or run the optimizer), so short, cheap queries never pay JIT overhead while long-running analytical queries can benefit from compiled expression evaluation.

questions.prompt: Given a large table joined to a tiny lookup table on an indexed key, which join strategy does the planner typically favor, and why?
choices: A nested loop using the index: for each row of the tiny table, an index probe into the large table is cheap, whereas building a hash table or sorting the large table first would cost more for no benefit
A hash join, always, regardless of table sizes
A merge join, because it is always the fastest option
Postgres always uses nested loop joins for every join

query.title: Join method selection
query.syntax: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM small_lookup l JOIN big_table b ON b.lookup_id = l.id;
query.explanation: The planner estimates the cost of each candidate join method (nested loop, hash, merge) for the specific tables and predicates involved and picks the cheapest. Nested loop with an inner index scan wins when one side is small and the other has a usable index, since it avoids the up-front cost of building a hash table or sorting the big side; a hash join tends to win when both sides are large with no helpful index, and a merge join wins when both sides are already sorted (or cheaply sortable) on the join key.

questions.prompt: A sort or hash operation in a plan needs more memory than `work_mem` allows. What happens?
choices: The operation spills intermediate data to temporary files on disk and continues in a slower, disk-based algorithm rather than failing
The query fails immediately with an out-of-memory error
Postgres automatically raises work_mem for that one query
The planner silently returns incomplete results

query.title: work_mem and disk spills
query.syntax:
SET work_mem = '64MB';
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT ... ORDER BY ...;  -- look for "Sort Method: external merge  Disk:"
query.explanation: work_mem bounds how much memory a single sort, hash, or similar operation is allowed to use before Postgres falls back to writing batches to temporary files on disk and merging them, a strategy that still produces correct results but is considerably slower than an in-memory sort/hash. EXPLAIN ANALYZE will show "Sort Method: external merge Disk: NkB" when this happens, and note each sort/hash node in a plan gets its own work_mem allotment, so a query with several such nodes running concurrently can use several multiples of the configured value.

questions.prompt: Because the OS page cache also caches file data independently of Postgres, a page that is "cached" often physically exists in memory twice: once in shared_buffers and once in the OS cache, an effect commonly called double buffering.

query.title: shared_buffers and OS cache
query.syntax: shared_buffers = 4GB
query.explanation: Postgres reads and writes heap/index files through the normal OS filesystem interface rather than bypassing the kernel, so any page it reads into shared_buffers typically also lingers in the OS's own page cache from that same read. This double buffering is a known inefficiency of Postgres's buffer manager design, and it is one reason shared_buffers is conventionally tuned to a fraction of total RAM rather than nearly all of it, leaving the rest of memory for the OS cache to hold whatever spills out of shared_buffers.

questions.prompt: `effective_cache_size` sounds like it allocates memory, but what does it actually do?
choices: Nothing is allocated; it is purely a hint telling the planner how much memory is likely available for caching data, which biases cost estimates toward or away from index usage
It sets a hard cap on total memory Postgres can use
It reserves that much RAM exclusively for shared_buffers
It controls how much memory autovacuum can use

query.title: effective_cache_size
query.syntax: effective_cache_size = 12GB
query.explanation: Unlike shared_buffers or work_mem, effective_cache_size never causes Postgres to actually reserve or allocate memory, it exists solely as an input to the planner's cost model, an estimate of the total memory (Postgres buffers plus the OS filesystem cache combined) likely available to cache the data being queried. Setting it too low makes the planner overly pessimistic about how often a repeated index lookup will hit cache versus disk, biasing plans toward sequential scans even on a machine with plenty of RAM to cache the working set.

questions.prompt: Why is lowering `random_page_cost` from its default of 4 toward something like 1.1 commonly recommended when a database’s storage is SSD/NVMe rather than spinning disk?
choices: The default ratio to seq_page_cost models the extra seek penalty of random I/O on rotating disks; SSDs have far less of a random-access penalty, so a lower ratio stops the planner from over-favoring sequential scans to avoid "expensive" random access that is no longer actually expensive
random_page_cost has no effect on plan choice, only on logging
Lowering it disables index scans entirely
It changes how data is physically stored on disk

query.title: random_page_cost tuning
query.syntax: SET random_page_cost = 1.1;
query.explanation: The planner’s cost model charges seq_page_cost (default 1) per sequentially-read page and random_page_cost (default 4) per randomly-accessed page, a ratio that models spinning-disk seek latency. An index scan does mostly random page accesses, so an inflated random_page_cost can make the planner prefer a sequential scan even when an index scan would touch far fewer pages overall; on SSD-backed storage where random and sequential access costs are much closer together, lowering random_page_cost closer to 1 lets the cost model reflect that and choose index scans more readily where they are actually cheaper.

questions.prompt: A server has `autovacuum_max_workers = 3` and 20 tables all become eligible for autovacuum around the same time. What happens?
choices: Only 3 tables get an autovacuum worker at once; the rest queue and wait their turn as workers free up
All 20 tables are vacuumed simultaneously regardless of the setting
Autovacuum refuses to run at all until the setting is raised to 20
The setting only limits manual VACUUM, not autovacuum

query.title: autovacuum_max_workers
query.syntax:
autovacuum_max_workers = 3
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'autovacuum worker';
query.explanation: autovacuum_max_workers caps how many autovacuum worker processes can run concurrently across the whole cluster, not per table or per database. If more tables are due than there are free worker slots, the excess simply wait, and if a handful of workers get tied up on very large tables for a long time, smaller-but-still-overdue tables elsewhere can be starved of attention, which is one reason a busy multi-database cluster often needs this raised beyond the default of 3.

questions.prompt: What is a "multixact ID" used for, and why can it also suffer a wraparound-style problem similar to regular transaction IDs?
choices: It represents a set of transaction IDs that jointly hold a shared row lock, and because multixact IDs are also a bounded counter, they must be periodically frozen/vacuumed away just like regular XIDs, or the cluster can hit multixact wraparound
It is an alternate name for a two-phase-commit transaction
It only appears in logical replication and never affects vacuum
It is a deprecated feature with no modern relevance

query.title: Multixact IDs
query.syntax: SELECT datminmxid FROM pg_database;
query.explanation: A single row can be locked (not exclusively, but for share) by more than one transaction at once, more than a single xmax field can represent, so Postgres records that set of holders as a multixact ID and stores that ID in the tuple’s xmax instead. Multixact IDs are their own bounded, wrapping counter with their own storage, so, like ordinary XIDs, old multixacts have to be frozen away by vacuum, and a workload with heavy concurrent row-level locking that outpaces vacuum can hit "multixact wraparound" protection kicking in, distinct from but analogous to ordinary XID wraparound.

questions.prompt: In `pg_stat_bgwriter`, a high `buffers_backend` relative to `buffers_clean` and `buffers_checkpoint` suggests what?
choices: Backend processes are frequently having to write out dirty buffers themselves to make room for new pages, rather than the background writer or checkpointer keeping ahead of demand
The database has too few tables
Replication is broken
The value has no operational meaning

query.title: pg_stat_bgwriter
query.syntax: SELECT buffers_clean, buffers_backend, buffers_checkpoint FROM pg_stat_bgwriter;
query.explanation: Ideally, the background writer proactively writes out dirty buffers ahead of time (buffers_clean) and checkpoints handle the rest on their own schedule (buffers_checkpoint), so a backend process needing a free buffer almost always finds a clean one ready. When buffers_backend is large, backends are frequently forced to write a dirty buffer out themselves on the critical path of needing a new one, which directly adds latency to whatever query triggered it, a common trigger for tuning bgwriter settings or checkpoint frequency.

questions.prompt: How does a `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expression) STORED` column differ from just computing that expression in every SELECT?
choices: Its value is computed once and physically stored on disk whenever the row is written, so it can be indexed directly and read without recomputation, but it cannot be written to directly
It behaves identically to a VIEW column with zero storage cost
It is computed fresh on every read and never stored
It can be updated directly like any normal column

query.title: Generated columns
query.explanation: A STORED generated column is computed at INSERT/UPDATE time from the other columns in that same row and written to disk like a regular column, which means it can be indexed and read cheaply, unlike recomputing an expression in every query. The tradeoff is it can only depend on other columns of the same row, and any direct INSERT/UPDATE that tries to supply its own value is rejected, Postgres always recomputes it itself.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of `CREATE DOMAIN positive_int AS integer CHECK (VALUE > 0)` over just adding a CHECK constraint to every column that needs this rule?
choices: The validation rule is defined once and attached to the type itself, so every column or function that uses the domain automatically enforces it, instead of the rule being copy-pasted across every table definition
Domains are strictly faster at runtime than CHECK constraints
Domains can only be used for text columns
Domains automatically create an index on every column that uses them

query.title: Domains
query.syntax:
CREATE DOMAIN positive_int AS integer CHECK (VALUE > 0);
CREATE TABLE t (qty positive_int);
query.explanation: A domain is a named subtype with its own constraints layered on a base type, so once you define it, using that domain as a column type (or as a function’s parameter/return type) automatically carries the constraint along, giving one authoritative definition of "what a positive_int is" instead of re-declaring CHECK (qty > 0) on every table that needs an always-positive quantity, and a future rule change only has to happen in one ALTER DOMAIN statement.

questions.prompt: Why does `WHERE tags @> ARRAY['urgent']` benefit from a GIN index on `tags` while `WHERE tags = ARRAY['urgent', 'bug']` (exact equality) does not use it the same way?
choices: GIN’s inverted-index structure is built to answer "contains element X" efficiently by looking up postings for that element; whole-array equality is a different comparison the GIN opclass for arrays does not accelerate the same way
GIN indexes cannot be built on array columns at all
Both queries use the GIN index identically
GIN indexes only support text columns

query.title: GIN and array containment
query.syntax:
CREATE INDEX ON t USING gin (tags);
SELECT * FROM t WHERE tags @> ARRAY['urgent'];
query.explanation: The GIN operator class for arrays decomposes an array into its individual elements and indexes "which rows contain element X", which directly answers containment (`@>`), overlap (`&&`), and element-existence queries by looking up postings for the relevant elements and intersecting/unioning the results. Whole-array equality compares the entire ordered array as one unit, a different question the containment-oriented opclass is not structured to answer via the same posting-list lookups, so it typically falls back to a sequential scan instead.

questions.prompt: In Postgres full text search, what is the difference between what `@@` determines and what `ts_rank()` adds?
choices: @@ answers a yes/no match against the document; ts_rank() separately computes a relevance score from term frequency and lexeme weight/position, letting you order matching rows by relevance rather than just filtering them
ts_rank replaces the need for a tsvector column entirely
@@ and ts_rank are interchangeable and return the same type
ts_rank only works on unindexed columns

query.title: Full text search ranking
query.syntax:
SELECT title, ts_rank(body_tsv, query) AS rank
FROM docs, to_tsquery('postgres & index') query
WHERE body_tsv @@ query
ORDER BY rank DESC;
query.explanation: The @@ match operator is a boolean test, a document either matches a tsquery or it does not, and that is all a GIN index on the tsvector accelerates directly. ts_rank() (and ts_rank_cd()) is a separate scoring function that looks at how many matching lexemes appear, their assigned weights (via setweight(), e.g. giving a title higher weight than body text), and, for the cover-density variant, how close together they appear, producing a float you can ORDER BY to surface the most relevant matches first.

questions.prompt: How does the `pg_trgm` extension make `ILIKE '%searchterm%'` or fuzzy similarity queries index-able, when a plain B-tree cannot help with a leading wildcard?
choices: It breaks each string into overlapping three-character sequences (trigrams) and builds a GIN or GiST index over those, so a search can be answered by matching trigrams of the search term instead of scanning every row
It converts the column to a full-text tsvector automatically
It rewrites the query to remove the wildcard entirely
It only accelerates exact equality, not pattern matching
