query.title: pg_trgm trigram indexes
query.explanation: A B-tree index on a text column can only help a LIKE/ILIKE pattern anchored at the start ('smith%'), because leaf entries are sorted by full string prefix. pg_trgm instead decomposes strings into overlapping 3-character trigrams and indexes those, so a query with a wildcard anywhere in the pattern (or a similarity search via the % operator) can be answered by finding rows sharing enough trigrams with the search term, then double-checking the actual match, which is also the basis for fuzzy matching via similarity().

questions.prompt: An extension you installed a while ago has a newer version available with bugfixes. What is the correct way to pick it up?
choices: ALTER EXTENSION extname UPDATE, which runs the specific migration script for upgrading from the currently-installed version to the target version, rather than reinstalling from scratch
DROP EXTENSION followed by CREATE EXTENSION, which is always safe and equivalent
Extensions update themselves automatically on server restart
You must dump and restore the whole database

query.title: ALTER EXTENSION UPDATE
query.syntax: ALTER EXTENSION my_ext UPDATE TO '2.0';
query.explanation: Extensions ship a chain of small SQL migration scripts between consecutive versions (a script from 1.0 to 1.1, another from 1.1 to 2.0), and ALTER EXTENSION UPDATE walks that chain to bring the installed version up to the target, preserving dependent objects like views or foreign keys that reference the extension’s types. Dropping and recreating the extension instead would fail (or silently lose data) if anything in the database depends on objects the extension defines, which the versioned update path avoids.

questions.prompt: A parent table has a child table referencing it with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, and the child table is large with no index on the foreign key column. What happens when you delete one parent row?
choices: Postgres must find and delete every matching child row, and without an index on the foreign key column it does so via a sequential scan of the entire child table
The cascade delete is skipped automatically if there is no index
ON DELETE CASCADE requires an index and refuses to be created without one
Only the parent row is deleted; children are cleaned up later by autovacuum

query.title: Cascade deletes without an index
query.syntax:
ALTER TABLE child ADD CONSTRAINT fk FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES parent (id) ON DELETE CASCADE;
-- missing: CREATE INDEX ON child (parent_id);
query.explanation: Enforcing ON DELETE CASCADE requires Postgres to locate every child row referencing the deleted parent, and it does that with whatever access path is available; without an index on the foreign key column, that means a full sequential scan of the (potentially huge) child table for every single parent delete. This is a very common, easy-to-miss performance trap, Postgres does not require or automatically create an index on a foreign key column the way a primary key gets one implicitly, and the fix is simply to add one explicitly.

questions.prompt: What does `SELECT * FROM big_table TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1)` do?
choices: Returns a random sample of roughly 1% of the table by randomly selecting whole storage pages, as opposed to BERNOULLI which samples individual rows independently
Returns exactly the first 1% of rows in insertion order
Limits the query to 1 second of execution time
Samples 1 row from the table regardless of size

query.title: TABLESAMPLE
query.syntax:
SELECT * FROM big_table TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM (1);
SELECT * FROM big_table TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (1);
query.explanation: TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM samples at the page level, randomly deciding whether to include each block and then returning all rows on included blocks, which is very fast because it can skip most of the table’s I/O entirely, but the sample can be skewed if rows with similar characteristics are physically clustered on the same pages. BERNOULLI instead independently decides per-row whether to include it, giving a more statistically clean random sample at the cost of still having to visit every row to make that decision.

questions.prompt: pg_stat_statements normalizes `SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 5` and `SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 999` into the same tracked entry. What about `SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (1,2,3)` versus `SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (1,2)`?
choices: They are typically tracked as separate entries, because normalization does not collapse a variable-length IN-list into a single canonical shape the way a single scalar parameter is collapsed
They are always merged into one entry regardless of list length
pg_stat_statements cannot track any query containing IN at all
IN-lists are converted to JOINs before normalization

query.title: Query normalization limits
query.syntax: SELECT query, calls FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE query LIKE '%WHERE id IN%';
query.explanation: Query normalization in pg_stat_statements replaces each individual constant with a parameter placeholder based on the parsed query structure, but an IN-list with a different number of elements produces a structurally different parse tree, so it is not folded into the same normalized entry as a list of a different length. This is a known practical wrinkle: an application that builds ad hoc IN-lists of varying size fragments its statistics across many pg_stat_statements rows instead of consolidating into one, which is one reason to prefer `= ANY($1::int[])` with a single array parameter when tracking that query’s aggregate cost matters.

questions.prompt: What are "hint bits" on a heap tuple, and why does the first read of a freshly-committed row sometimes trigger an extra write?
choices: Hint bits cache the outcome of a previous visibility check directly on the tuple so future readers can skip re-checking transaction status against the commit log; setting them for the first time dirties the page even though no user-visible data changed
Hint bits are a debugging feature with no effect on production behavior
They store the query planner’s hints for that specific row
They are only relevant to TOAST-ed columns

query.title: Hint bits
query.syntax: -- not directly queryable via SQL; internal to the tuple header
query.explanation: Determining whether a tuple’s inserting or deleting transaction actually committed normally means consulting the commit log (pg_xact/clog), extra work worth avoiding on every read of the same row. The first reader to do that check caches the answer as a "hint bit" set directly in the tuple’s header, so later readers can trust the bit instead of re-checking, but writing that bit for the first time modifies the page in memory and marks it dirty, which is why a purely read-only query against freshly-written data can still generate write I/O later when that dirtied page is flushed.

questions.prompt: A parameterized prepared statement is executed repeatedly with different parameter values. What changes about how it is planned after the fifth execution?
choices: Postgres starts considering a generic plan (built without knowing the specific parameter values) and switches to using it going forward if its estimated cost is not noticeably worse than the average cost of the custom plans built for the first five executions
Nothing changes; the exact same plan from the first execution is always reused forever
A brand new plan is generated from scratch on every single execution regardless of history
The statement is automatically converted into a stored procedure

query.title: Generic vs custom prepared plans
query.syntax:
PREPARE get_order (int) AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1;
EXECUTE get_order(5);  -- repeat with different ids
query.explanation: For the first five executions of a prepared statement, Postgres plans using the actual parameter values each time (a "custom" plan, potentially different and better-optimized per call). Starting from the sixth, it compares the average cost of those custom plans against a single "generic" plan built without assuming specific values, and switches permanently to the generic plan if it is not meaningfully worse, trading a small amount of per-call optimality for skipping replanning on every execution; a workload where parameter values wildly change the optimal plan shape can suffer once it locks onto an unsuitable generic plan.

questions.prompt: Autovacuum deciding to VACUUM a table and autovacuum deciding to ANALYZE it are governed by separate threshold settings, so a table can be vacuumed without being re-analyzed, or vice versa, depending on how much of its data changed.

query.title: Separate vacuum vs analyze thresholds
query.syntax:
autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.2
autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.1
query.explanation: Autovacuum tracks two independent counters and threshold pairs: one for dead tuples (governing VACUUM, via autovacuum_vacuum_threshold/scale_factor) and one for rows changed since the last ANALYZE (via autovacuum_analyze_threshold/scale_factor). Because ANALYZE’s default scale factor is lower, a table often gets re-analyzed more frequently than it gets vacuumed, and it is entirely possible for one to fire without the other in the same autovacuum pass, which matters when diagnosing why statistics went stale despite the table clearly having been vacuumed recently, or vice versa.

questions.prompt: What does `pg_stat_replication.replay_lag` (as opposed to `write_lag` or `flush_lag`) measure on the primary?
choices: The time between a transaction committing on the primary and that change actually being replayed (applied and visible to queries) on the standby
The network latency between primary and standby
How long the primary has been running
The disk space difference between primary and standby

query.title: Replication lag components
query.syntax: SELECT application_name, write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;
query.explanation: Postgres breaks standby lag into three stages: write_lag (WAL received and written on the standby), flush_lag (that WAL made durable on the standby’s disk), and replay_lag (the WAL actually replayed, making the change queryable). A standby can have low write/flush lag but a much larger replay_lag if it is CPU- or I/O-bound applying changes, which is the number that directly answers "if I query the replica right now, how far behind the primary is what I will see."

questions.prompt: Why must `wal_level` be set to at least `replica` (not `minimal`) before you can set up streaming physical replication, and to `logical` before logical replication?
choices: Each higher wal_level records additional information in WAL beyond the bare minimum needed for crash recovery: replica adds what a standby needs to reconstruct changes, logical adds what decoding needs to reconstruct row-level changes
wal_level only controls compression, not content
minimal WAL level is actually sufficient for logical replication, this is a common misconception
wal_level has no relationship to replication at all

query.title: wal_level and replication
query.syntax: wal_level = logical   -- postgresql.conf, requires restart
query.explanation: At minimal, Postgres skips WAL-logging some operations it can reconstruct another way, relying on the fact there is no standby to keep in sync, which saves overhead but means the resulting WAL stream is insufficient to rebuild a replica’s state from. replica restores that full logging so streaming replication has everything it needs, and logical goes further, additionally recording enough information (like old row values, depending on replica identity) for logical decoding to reconstruct row-level operations rather than just physical page changes.

questions.prompt: Why would you lower a table’s `FILLFACTOR` below the default of 100 for a table that receives frequent UPDATEs?
choices: Leaving free space on each page at insert time gives room for later HOT updates to place the new row version on the same page, avoiding new index entries
Lowering FILLFACTOR makes SELECT queries return faster
FILLFACTOR only affects index pages, never heap pages
FILLFACTOR determines the maximum row size allowed

query.title: FILLFACTOR and HOT updates
query.syntax: ALTER TABLE t SET (fillfactor = 70);
query.explanation: FILLFACTOR controls how full INSERT (and CLUSTER/VACUUM FULL rewrites) pack each page, leaving the remainder as reserved free space. A table updated often benefits from leaving that headroom, because a HOT update needs room on the same page to place the new tuple version; a page packed to 100% full has nowhere to put an updated row without spilling to a different page, which forces a regular (non-HOT) update that must also update every index referencing that row.

questions.prompt: A query filters with `WHERE lower(email) = 'someone@example.com'`. What kind of index actually helps here, and why does a plain index on `email` not?
choices: An expression index built on lower(email) itself, since a plain B-tree on the raw column is sorted by the unmodified value and cannot satisfy a predicate on a function of that column
Any index on email automatically covers this, functions are transparent to the planner
A GIN index is required for any function-based predicate
This case can only be solved with a generated column, never an index directly

query.title: Expression (functional) indexes
query.syntax:
CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email));
SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'someone@example.com';
query.explanation: An index is built and sorted according to whatever expression you give CREATE INDEX, which is normally just the bare column, but does not have to be. Because lower(email) is a different value than email itself, a plain index on the column has no way to help a predicate on the lowercased form; creating the index directly on the expression lower(email) makes Postgres maintain an index sorted by that computed value, which the planner can then match against a query using the identical expression.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a trigger to be `CONSTRAINT TRIGGER ... DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED`?
choices: It is a constraint trigger whose firing can be postponed to COMMIT time, rather than firing immediately after the triggering statement, which lets it validate the final state of a transaction rather than each intermediate step
It is a normal trigger that only runs on DDL
It is a trigger that fires once per database restart
It is a trigger with no functional difference from a regular AFTER trigger

query.title: Constraint triggers and deferral
query.syntax:
CREATE CONSTRAINT TRIGGER check_balance
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE ON accounts
DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION check_balance_fn();
query.explanation: A regular AFTER trigger always fires right after its triggering statement within the transaction, with no option to postpone it. A CONSTRAINT TRIGGER is specifically designed to participate in the same deferral machinery as DEFERRABLE constraints, letting you mark it INITIALLY DEFERRED so it only runs at COMMIT, useful when a business rule can be legitimately violated between two statements in a transaction but must hold once that transaction actually commits.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `pg_cancel_backend(pid)` and `pg_terminate_backend(pid)`?
choices: pg_cancel_backend asks the target backend to abort its current query while keeping the session/connection open; pg_terminate_backend forcibly ends the entire backend process and its connection
They are exact synonyms provided for convenience
pg_cancel_backend only works on the current session's own backend
pg_terminate_backend only cancels the query, never the connection

query.title: Cancel vs terminate backend
query.syntax:
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(1234);
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(1234);
query.explanation: pg_cancel_backend sends a SIGINT-equivalent signal that interrupts whatever the target backend is currently running, rolling back the current transaction/query but leaving the client's session connected and free to run another statement. pg_terminate_backend is more forceful, it disconnects the client entirely, which is what you reach for when a session is stuck in a way that a plain query cancel does not clear, at the cost of the client needing to reconnect.

questions.prompt: What is a composite type created with `CREATE TYPE address AS (street text, city text, zip text)`, structurally?
choices: A structured row type with named, typed fields that can be used as a column type, function parameter/return type, or nested inside another composite/array
An alias with no structure, equivalent to text
A type that can only be used as a table's primary key
A synonym for a JSON column

query.title: Composite types
query.explanation: Every table in Postgres implicitly defines a composite type matching its own row shape, and CREATE TYPE ... AS lets you define that same kind of structured, multi-field type standalone, without a backing table, for use as a column type, a function’s parameter or return type, or nested within an array or another composite. Accessing a field means parenthesizing the composite value first, since `home.city` would otherwise be parsed as a table-qualified column reference.

questions.prompt: Why does `SELECT int4range(1,5) = int4range(1,4,'[]')` evaluate to true, even though the literal bounds look different?
choices: Discrete range types are canonicalized to a standard form before comparison, converting an inclusive upper bound to the equivalent exclusive one, so two textually different but logically identical ranges compare equal
Postgres range equality only checks the lower bound
This actually evaluates to false; ranges with different bound literals are never equal
Range types cannot be compared with = at all

query.title: Range type canonicalization
query.syntax:
SELECT int4range(1,5);       -- [1,5)
SELECT int4range(1,4,'[]');  -- also [1,5) after canonicalization
query.explanation: For a discrete range type like int4range (built on a type with a well-defined "next value," unlike a continuous type such as numrange), Postgres normalizes the range into a canonical form, conventionally lower-inclusive/upper-exclusive, immediately on construction, converting [1,4] into the equivalent [1,5). That normalization is exactly why two ranges written with different inclusivity but the same actual set of integers compare as equal, and why range equality/containment behaves consistently regardless of which bound style the caller happened to use.

questions.prompt: A parent table's primary key is updated on a row referenced by a large child table with `ON UPDATE CASCADE`. What lock-related cost does this share with an uncascaded, unindexed `ON DELETE CASCADE`?
choices: Postgres must locate every child row referencing the old key value to update their foreign key column, which without an index on that column means scanning the entire child table while holding locks for the duration
ON UPDATE CASCADE never needs to touch the child table at all
It is always faster than ON DELETE CASCADE regardless of indexing
It only affects the parent table, never the child

query.title: Cascade update cost
query.syntax: ALTER TABLE child ADD CONSTRAINT fk FOREIGN KEY (parent_code) REFERENCES parent (code) ON UPDATE CASCADE;
query.explanation: Changing a referenced parent key value under ON UPDATE CASCADE requires finding and rewriting every child row that pointed at the old value, structurally the same "find all matching children" problem as ON DELETE CASCADE, and it pays the same cost if there is no index on the child’s foreign key column: a full scan of the child table, with row locks held on every matched row until the updating transaction finishes, a good reason to avoid mutable natural keys as foreign key targets in the first place.

questions.prompt: A table has both a `BEFORE INSERT FOR EACH ROW` trigger and a `BEFORE INSERT FOR EACH STATEMENT` trigger for a multi-row INSERT. In what order do they fire?
choices: The statement-level trigger fires once, before any row-level trigger invocations begin; then the row-level trigger fires once per inserted row
The row-level trigger fires once per row first, then the statement-level trigger fires once at the very end regardless of BEFORE/AFTER
They fire simultaneously and their relative order is undefined
Only one of the two trigger levels can exist on the same table at once

query.title: Statement vs row trigger firing order
query.syntax:
CREATE TRIGGER stmt_trig BEFORE INSERT ON t FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION f1();
CREATE TRIGGER row_trig BEFORE INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION f2();
query.explanation: FOR EACH STATEMENT triggers fire exactly once around the whole statement, while FOR EACH ROW triggers fire once per affected row; for BEFORE triggers, the statement-level one runs first (before any rows are processed), then the row-level trigger runs for each row in turn, and the equivalent AFTER STATEMENT trigger runs once at the very end after every row-level AFTER trigger invocation has completed. Knowing this ordering matters for a common pattern where the statement-level trigger initializes something that the row-level trigger then updates per row.

questions.prompt: `unnest(some_array)` used in a FROM clause and `array_agg(column)` used with GROUP BY are, in a sense, inverse operations. What does `unnest` specifically do?
choices: It expands an array value into a set of rows, one per element, which lets you join against, filter, or aggregate individual array elements using ordinary relational operations
It sorts an array in place without changing its structure
It converts an array to a single JSON string
It removes duplicate elements from an array

query.title: unnest and array_agg
query.explanation: unnest is a set-returning function that turns one array value into one row per element, letting you treat array contents as if they were a normal joined table, filterable, groupable, aggregatable with plain SQL instead of array-specific operators. array_agg does the reverse: it collapses multiple rows (typically grouped) back into a single array value, so the common pattern of unnesting to manipulate elements and then re-aggregating is a standard way to apply row-oriented SQL logic to what started out as array data.
